positives: Decision 2 fails closed: session with NULL yandex_login is rejected by RequireAuth (401 session_identity_missing) rather than defaulting to a permissive identity.
Decision 1 rejects the 'login in a separate cookie' alternative for the right reason (client-controlled value) and reads role from the DB per request instead of trusting a client claim.
Decision 3 separates has_access from request history, so revocation does not depend on rewriting an approval record.
Decision 10 (has_access || role=='admin') removes the self-lockout footgun without adding a special case for 'self'.

All new persistence goes through GORM/database-sql with placeholders; the design introduces no string-concatenated SQL and no new dependencies (no new CVE surface). Client dependencies are pinned at vite 5.4.21 in package-lock.json, past the 5.4.x dev-server CVEs.

Acceptance criteria include an explicit 'no SMTP secret in the repository' check, and the risk table names the missing gitleaks/pre-commit hook. No hardcoded credentials found in tracked files (git grep for API_KEY/SECRET/PASSWORD/TOKEN literals is clean apart from the dev defaults in finding SEC-15).

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 6 + User-Spec Deviations ('Сужение относительно US-13'); grounded in server/internal/handler/http.go:22-70 and client/src/pages/Panel.jsx:190, 230-278
findings.description: The access gate is enforced only on the new /api/v1/access/* and /api/v1/admin/* contour. All actual product data stays behind /api/v1/users/{userID}/*, which has no authentication of any kind: handleUsers takes userID straight from the path and never looks at a cookie. The client derives userID from profile.login (Panel.jsx:190), so the identifier an attacker needs is a public Yandex login. Consequence: a user who was never approved, or whose access was explicitly revoked, retains full unauthenticated read/write on every user's settings, chats and calculations, and can drive POST /api/v1/users/{any}/market-feedback, which spends the DeepSeek API key. US-10 ('доступ отзывается') and the user-spec 'Why' ('уметь отзывать доступ у конкретного пользователя') are therefore not achieved at the API layer at all - the shipped control is a UI gate. The residual-risk documentation is partially honest but incomplete: the deviation note says the user 'может напрямую читать и писать данные расчётов любого пользователя, как и до этой фичи', but it never states that this nullifies the revocation requirement, it is absent from the Risks table, absent from Acceptance Criteria, and the Solution section still asserts 'Доступ к рабочему интерфейсу панели становится явным состоянием пользователя'. The user's acceptance of the scope reduces the business urgency, not the technical severity.
findings.recommendation: Do not soften the wording - state in Solution, Risks and User-Spec Deviations that after this feature access revocation has no effect on the data API, and that any authenticated Yandex user (approved or not) plus any anonymous internet caller retains full CRUD over all tenants' data. If the endpoints truly stay out of scope, add a compensating control that is in scope and cheap: put RequireAuth + a has_access check in front of /api/v1/users/ in cmd/main.go as a single middleware wrap (the middleware is already being built in Task 5) and assert userID from the path equals the login in context. That is roughly 15 lines and closes IDOR, forced browsing and the unauthenticated LLM spend in one move. If it is deferred, file it as a tracked debt item with an owner and add an acceptance criterion recording the accepted residual risk verbatim.

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 11 / Data Models (users table); grounded in server/internal/repository/postgres.go:550-555 and :140, :233, :363
findings.description: The feature moves role and has_access onto the users table, but rows in that table can already be created by an unauthenticated caller: upsertUser(tx, userID) is invoked from UpsertSettings/CreateChat/AppendCalculation with the userID taken verbatim from the unauthenticated path. An anonymous attacker can therefore inject unlimited rows with arbitrary attacker-chosen identifiers directly into the table that is now the access-control source of truth and the backing store for GET /api/v1/admin/users. Concrete consequences the tech-spec does not consider: (a) the admin console is flooded with attacker-controlled strings, and an attacker can plant a lookalike login (homoglyph or trailing-space variant of a real user) to social-engineer an admin into ticking the box on the wrong row; (b) US-7's invariant 'список содержит всех, кто когда-либо входил' is false - the list contains anyone anybody ever named in a URL; (c) unbounded row growth against an unpaginated ListUsers (see SEC-13). The one thing that keeps this from being direct unauthenticated privilege escalation is that upsertUser uses clause.OnConflict{DoNothing:true} and userModel carries only ID and CreatedAt, so it cannot overwrite role/has_access - but the tech-spec never states this as a required invariant, so a later change that adds email or role to userModel and switches to DoUpdates converts this into instant anonymous admin self-promotion.
findings.recommendation: Record as an explicit, tested invariant in the tech-spec: upsertUser and any userModel change must never write role or has_access, and userModel must not gain those columns. Add a repository contract test asserting that upsertUser on an existing admin row leaves role and has_access untouched (the spec already plans EnsureUser's equivalent test - extend it to the legacy path). Separately, either gate /api/v1/users/ (see SEC-01) or have ListUsers return only rows that have a login-derived provenance marker (e.g. a created_via column set to 'oauth' by EnsureUser) so the admin console never displays anonymously injected identifiers.

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 1 / 'Вход' in Architecture (HandleYandexLogin listed as an identity source); grounded in server/internal/handler/auth.go:42-97
findings.description: POST /auth/yandex accepts an access_token supplied by the client in the request body and mints a server session around it, with no verification that the token was issued to this application. Today the blast radius is 'a session in a panel anyone could use anyway'. This tech-spec changes that: the session's identity - and through users.role, its administrative authority - is now derived by calling login.yandex.ru/info with exactly that attacker-supplied token. Any Yandex OAuth access token for an administrator's account, issued to any Yandex application whatsoever (a token stolen from an unrelated third-party app the admin authorized, a token leaked in a log or Referer), can be replayed into POST /auth/yandex to obtain a fully privileged admin session in PoshivOn. This is the classic OAuth token-substitution / confused-deputy pattern. Two aggravating details in the same handler: expires_in is read from the client body (auth.go:64-68), so the caller chooses the server-side lifetime of the access half of the session; and refresh_token is also accepted from the body (auth.go:84-86) and stored for later use against Yandex.
findings.recommendation: Do not build identity on this endpoint without audience verification. Preferred: delete POST /auth/yandex and keep only the confidential-client code flow (POST /auth/yandex/code), which is what the client already uses (buildYandexAuthUrl emits response_type=code). If it must stay, verify the token audience server-side - reject unless the client_id returned by login.yandex.ru/info equals cfg.YandexClientID - and ignore client-supplied expires_in and refresh_token (derive lifetime from the verified token or a fixed server constant). Add an acceptance criterion: a session created from a token issued to a different client_id is rejected with 401.

findings.location: tech-spec 'Контракт API' + Decision 9; grounded in server/internal/handler/cors.go:25-35, server/internal/config/config.go:66-69, server/internal/handler/http.go:226-239
findings.description: The two new state-changing endpoints - POST /api/v1/admin/users/{login}/access and POST /api/v1/access/requests - are authenticated purely by ambient cookies. The tech-spec contains no CSRF control of any kind: no anti-CSRF token, no Origin/Referer allowlist check, no Content-Type enforcement (decodeJSON never inspects the header). The only thing standing between a hostile page and a silent privilege grant is COOKIE_SAMESITE, which comes from an unreviewed GitHub secret and defaults to 'Lax' in code (config.go:69) - and the CORS layer sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true for an allowlist of origins, i.e. the architecture explicitly anticipates cross-origin browser use, which requires SameSite=None and removes the protection entirely. SameSite=Lax also does not defend against a same-site attacker: any content injected on any subdomain of poshivon.ru can issue the POST. The target is the highest-value operation in the system: an attacker page loaded by a logged-in admin flips granted:true on the attacker's own login. Decision 9 discusses POST vs PATCH purely as a CORS-methods convenience and never reaches the CSRF question.
findings.recommendation: Add to RequireAuth, for all unsafe methods: reject unless the Origin header is present and in the configured allowlist (fall back to Referer host; reject when both absent), and require Content-Type: application/json exactly. Add a startup assertion that COOKIE_SAMESITE is not 'None' unless an explicit opt-in flag is set, and that COOKIE_SECURE is true whenever SameSite=None. Add acceptance criteria: a POST to /api/v1/admin/users/{login}/access with a foreign Origin returns 403 and does not change the flag; a POST with Content-Type: text/plain returns 415.

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 12 (modifies buildYandexAuthUrl); grounded in client/src/utils/yandexAuth.js:125-142
findings.description: buildYandexAuthUrl builds the Yandex authorize URL with response_type, client_id and redirect_uri only - there is no state parameter, and therefore no CSRF binding between the authorization request and the callback, and no PKCE. The callback handler accepts whatever code arrives. This permits login-CSRF and authorization-code injection: an attacker can cause a victim's browser to complete the OAuth callback with a code of the attacker's choosing, silently pinning the victim into an attacker-controlled session (everything the victim then enters - settings, order data, calculations - lands in the attacker's account), or the reverse depending on the flow chosen. Decision 12 edits this exact function to add scope=login:info login:email and does not add state, so the spec walks past the defect while standing on it. The impact rises with this feature because the session now carries a role.
findings.recommendation: In the same edit as the scope parameter: generate a 128-bit random state, store it in sessionStorage, include it in the authorize URL, and verify it in the /auth callback before POSTing the code to the server (reject and restart the flow on mismatch or absence). Add PKCE (code_challenge S256) if the Yandex app is ever converted to a public client. Add an acceptance criterion: a callback carrying a state that does not match the stored value never reaches POST /auth/yandex/code.

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 1 + Decision 12 (session identity redesign, scope widening); grounded in server/migrations/001_auth_sessions.up.sql:3-4, server/internal/handler/auth.go:93, 387-393, 421-452, server/internal/config/config.go:68
findings.description: The ya_access cookie carries the raw upstream Yandex OAuth access token to the browser, and oauth_sessions stores both yandex_access_token and the long-lived yandex_refresh_token as plaintext TEXT. Decision 12 widens the granted scope to login:info login:email, so a leaked token now also yields the user's email; the refresh token means a database read yields durable, renewable access to every user's Yandex identity, not a momentary one. COOKIE_SECURE defaults to false (config.go:68), so a misconfigured deploy transmits the token over cleartext. Critically, this exposure buys nothing: validateSession (auth.go:447) only compares the cookie value to the copy already stored in the row, so the cookie is functioning as an opaque session credential that happens to be a live third-party bearer token. This tech-spec is the moment the session row is being restructured, and Decision 1 evaluates identity storage without re-examining what else the row and the cookie hold.
findings.recommendation: Decouple while you are already touching the schema: put a fresh opaque random value (same generateToken path as the refresh cookie) in ya_access, store only its SHA-256 in oauth_sessions, and keep the Yandex access token server-side, encrypted at rest (AES-GCM with a key from env) or at minimum never sent to the browser. Refuse to start when COOKIE_SECURE is false and the redirect URI scheme is https. Add acceptance criteria: the ya_access cookie value does not appear in any Yandex API call made from the browser, and SELECT yandex_access_token FROM oauth_sessions does not return a usable bearer token in plaintext.

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 5 and 'Админские операции'; Data Models (access_requests PRIMARY KEY (user_id))
findings.description: The design has no audit trail for the security-relevant operations it introduces. The only record of who granted or revoked access is decided_by/decided_at on the single access_requests row - and Decision 5 makes that row PRIMARY KEY (user_id) and explicitly overwrites it on a re-request after rejection, destroying the previous decision. Revocation (granted:false) writes 'rejected' onto the same row, so the grant record is gone the moment access is taken away. Nothing in the spec logs authentication failures, RequireAuth/RequireAdmin denials, admin list reads, or SetAccess calls. After an incident there is no way to answer who granted access to whom, when, or from where - and no way to detect a credential-stuffing or session-replay campaign against the admin accounts (SEC-03, SEC-04 both produce zero signal).
findings.recommendation: Add an append-only table (access_audit: id, actor_login, target_login, action IN ('grant','revoke','request','decide'), old_value, new_value, ip, user_agent, created_at) written inside the same transaction as SetAccess and CreateRequest - MariaDB has no partial-index obstacle here, so Decision 5's trade-off does not apply. Add structured log lines for every 401 from RequireAuth and every 403 from RequireAdmin, including the login from context, path and source IP. Add acceptance criteria covering both. This also gives the feature a real answer to 'администратор ошибочно снял галочку' from the user-spec risk list.

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 7 and Task 2 (SMTPNotifier); Dependencies section
findings.description: Two gaps in the notifier design. (1) Transport: the spec fixes net/smtp and smtp.SendMail but specifies no port and no TLS policy. smtp.SendMail only upgrades opportunistically via STARTTLS when the server advertises it, and it cannot speak implicit TLS on port 465 at all - which is the default submission port for Yandex and Mail.ru SMTP, the likely providers here. The implementer is left to discover this at integration time and is one workaround away from relaying admin SMTP credentials and user PII in cleartext, or from a notifier that silently never sends. (2) Content: the message body is built from yandex_login and yandex_email, values that originate outside the trust boundary and are stored without normalization. The spec assigns net/mail validation to the configured recipient addresses only, not to these. If either value reaches a header (Subject, Reply-To, To) without CR/LF stripping, this is SMTP header injection (CWE-93) - an applicant can append Bcc recipients or replace the message seen by administrators, i.e. forge the approval request itself.
findings.recommendation: Specify in Decision 7: submission on port 587 with mandatory STARTTLS, and fail closed (log an error, do not send) if the server does not advertise STARTTLS; if 465 must be supported, use tls.Dial + smtp.NewClient explicitly. Never fall back to plaintext auth. Specify that login and email are stripped of \r and \n and truncated (login <= 255, email <= 255) before being formatted, that they appear in the body only - never in a header - and add a notifier test asserting that a login containing "\r\nBcc: attacker@evil.tld" produces a message with no additional header. Add SMTP_PASSWORD to the 'never logged, no default value' rule (see SEC-15).

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 9 / 'Контракт API' (POST /api/v1/admin/users/{login}/access); grounded in server/internal/handler/metrics.go:23-45
findings.description: The new admin route puts a user-controlled segment in the URL path, and every request passes through WithMetrics, which labels Prometheus series by normalized path. normalizePath's looksLikeID only collapses a segment that parses as an integer or is longer than 8 characters and contains a hyphen - a Yandex login such as 'ivanov' or 'admin1' matches neither and is emitted verbatim as a metric label value. Two consequences: user logins leak into Prometheus and into Grafana, which is published at https://poshivon.ru/grafana/ behind a single shared admin password; and because the same normalizer serves the unauthenticated /api/v1/users/<anything>/... route, any anonymous caller can mint unlimited distinct label values and drive Prometheus into unbounded memory growth - a remote, unauthenticated availability attack on the monitoring stack. The tech-spec introduces a second path-parameter route without checking the normalizer.
findings.recommendation: Register explicit route templates for the new contour and label metrics with the template, not the observed path (e.g. '/api/v1/admin/users/:login/access'). At minimum, change normalizePath so that any segment immediately following 'users' collapses to ':id' unconditionally, and cap the label set. Verify with: hit /api/v1/users/aaa/settings and /api/v1/users/bbb/settings, then confirm /metrics shows one series, not two.

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 7 ('в отдельной горутине') and 'Заявка' in Architecture
findings.description: There is no rate limiting anywhere in the design, and the request endpoint is the one that reaches out to a third party. The 409-on-pending rule is a uniqueness constraint, not a rate limit: after every rejection the user may immediately re-request (Decision 5 explicitly permits it), so a hostile applicant and an admin clicking reject produce an unbounded email loop against the admins' mailbox, from a path that costs the attacker one HTTP request. GET /api/v1/access/me and the admin endpoints have no throttling at all, so there is nothing slowing an attacker enumerating or replaying sessions (compare SEC-03/SEC-04, which have no detection either). Separately, 'в отдельной горутине' with no bound means one goroutine and one SMTP connection per request, with no timeout specified - an SMTP server that hangs accumulates goroutines and file descriptors until the process degrades.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-login and per-IP limiter on POST /api/v1/access/requests (e.g. 3/hour, 10/day) returning 429, plus a minimum cooldown before a re-request after a rejection. Replace the bare goroutine with a bounded queue (buffered channel of 8 + one worker); drop and log when full. Give SendMail an explicit context timeout (10s). Add acceptance criteria for the 429 and for the queue not growing under a stalled SMTP server.

findings.location: tech-spec Risks table ('writeAPIDomainError отдаёт клиенту err.Error() на 500') and Task 5; grounded in server/internal/handler/http.go:251-266
findings.description: The mitigation recorded in the Risks table - 'ветка 500 в новом контуре отдаёт фиксированный текст' - does not match the shape of the code being modified. writeAPIDomainError is a single shared function with one default branch that returns err.Error() to the client; Task 5 only adds 403 and 409 branches to it. There is no per-contour dispatch, so either the fix is not implementable as written, or the implementer bolts on a second error writer and the shared default keeps leaking raw driver text (table names, column names, constraint names, connection strings on dial failures) from the existing /api/v1/users/* contour, which is fully unauthenticated. The new schema makes leaked constraint names more interesting to an attacker (chk_users_role, fk_access_requests_user reveal the access-control model).
findings.recommendation: Fix it at the shared function rather than per contour: the default branch returns a constant 'internal error' body and logs err with a correlation id server-side; the same for the string-matching branches, which currently echo err.Error() as well. This is a smaller change than the per-contour split and removes the leak from the legacy routes too. Restate the Risks-table mitigation accordingly and keep the acceptance criterion, but broaden it to 'ни один ответ 500 не содержит текста внутренней ошибки'.

findings.location: tech-spec Decision 4 and Data Models ('Проставление администраторов'); User-Spec Deviations (US-6 extension)
findings.description: Privilege assignment is a manual, unverified, uninstrumented step. The UPDATE users SET role='admin' WHERE id IN ('ADMIN_LOGIN_1','ADMIN_LOGIN_2') inside migration 004 is guaranteed to be a no-op at the moment it runs - the spec itself states the rows do not exist until the admins have logged in - so the real privilege grant is a human running docker exec ... mariadb against production, with no record (see SEC-07), no verification step, and no acceptance criterion. Failure modes: a typo grants admin to a login the intended admin does not own (and per SEC-02, an attacker can pre-create any users row, so a mistyped id may already exist and look plausible); the step is silently skipped and the feature ships with zero admins and no one able to approve anything; the real admin logins get committed into a migration file in git, disclosing who to target. Nothing enforces US-6's 'ровно два'.
findings.recommendation: Move the admin set into configuration and reconcile it on startup: ADMIN_LOGINS as a comma-separated env var (it flows through the same five-hop pipeline Task 9 already builds), and on boot set role='admin' for those logins and role='user' for any other row currently holding 'admin'. That is idempotent, auditable, leaves no logins in git, survives a container rebuild, and makes 'exactly two admins' a startup invariant instead of a hope. The spec notes ADMIN_LOGINS was rejected by the user earlier - re-raise it with this reasoning. If it stays manual, at minimum add an acceptance criterion 'SELECT id FROM users WHERE role=\'admin\' returns exactly the two intended logins and nothing else', executed as part of Task 15.

findings.description: ListUsers(ctx) takes no pagination or filter arguments and the endpoint contract returns {items:[UserRecord]} for every row, each carrying login, email, role, has_access and timestamps. Combined with SEC-02 (anonymous row injection) this is both a PII-aggregation endpoint and an availability risk: response size and query cost grow with a number an unauthenticated attacker controls, and the admin UI renders all of it.
findings.recommendation: Add limit/offset (or keyset) parameters to ListUsers and a hard server-side cap (e.g. 200 per page) in the contract, and render paginated in AdminUsersSection. Emit email only where the admin needs it and consider masking it in the list view.

findings.description: The design specifies no validation or canonicalization for the {login} path segment. splitPath operates on r.URL.Path, which net/http has already percent-decoded, so a login containing %2F re-splits into extra segments and routes elsewhere or 404s, and a login with a trailing space or a Unicode homoglyph is accepted verbatim into the users lookup, the audit fields and the notification email (see SEC-02's lookalike-row scenario and SEC-08's header injection). There is no length bound before the value reaches a VARCHAR(255) column. GORM parameterization means this is not SQL injection, but it is an unvalidated identifier crossing three trust boundaries.
findings.recommendation: Validate the segment in the handler against ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,255}$ and return 400 otherwise; apply the same validation to the login persisted by EnsureUser. Use r.URL.EscapedPath() if raw segments ever matter for routing. Add a handler test for a login containing %2F and one containing a trailing space.

findings.location: tech-spec Task 9 (modifies docker-compose.yml, config.go); grounded in server/internal/config/config.go:60-64, docker-compose.yml (db service)
findings.description: config.go supplies silent fallback credentials: DB_USER defaults to 'poshivon' and DB_PASSWORD defaults to 'poshivon' via envOrDefault, and docker-compose.yml hardcodes MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: root, MARIADB_PASSWORD: poshivon and publishes 3306 to the host. Because envOrDefault falls back silently, the exact failure mode the tech-spec itself warns about for the new SMTP variables - a variable missing from the envs: allowlist in deploy.yml is lost without a sound - degrades the database connection to a well-known default password rather than failing the boot. Task 9 edits docker-compose.yml and config.go and does not address this.
findings.recommendation: Remove the defaults for DB_PASSWORD and DB_USER; return an error from config.Load when either is empty and APP_STORAGE is not memory, so a lost variable produces a crash-loop instead of a default-credentialed service. Apply the same rule to the new SMTP_PASSWORD (no default, never logged, redacted in any config dump). Drop the host port publish on the db service in docker-compose.yml, or bind it to 127.0.0.1.

findings.location: tech-spec Task 9 (modifies client/nginx.conf and the deploy.yml heredoc nginx config); grounded in client/nginx.conf:1-8, deploy/nginx.conf:7-17, .github/workflows/deploy.yml:130-233
findings.description: Neither nginx configuration sets any security header beyond X-Robots-Tag: no Content-Security-Policy, no Strict-Transport-Security (deploy/nginx.conf terminates TLS and still omits it), no X-Content-Type-Options, no X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors, no Referrer-Policy. The feature adds an administrative UI whose primary action is a single click that grants access, which makes clickjacking a directly exploitable path to privilege grant, and a Referrer-Policy default means the /auth callback URL carrying the OAuth code can leak in a Referer header to any third-party resource. Task 9 already opens both files to add /auth/refresh proxying, so the marginal cost is a few lines.
findings.recommendation: In the same task add, to both configs: Strict-Transport-Security max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin, and a CSP with frame-ancestors 'none' (start report-only if the SPA needs tuning). Verify with curl -I against the deployed host in Task 15.
